intent: Cut a program along the seams where decisions change, so each module holds one coherent responsibility and reaches other modules only through narrow, stable contracts.
problem: A module whose parts change for different reasons, or that shares data structures with many others, turns every change into a change everywhere: recompilation ripples, tests need unrelated fixtures, and the cost of editing one part is the cost of editing the whole graph.
context: Two complementary criteria. Cohesion is about what is inside a module: put the parts that change together in the same place. Coupling is about what crosses between modules: prefer parameter passing and contracts over shared globals, so a change propagates to as few modules as possible. The decisive question when drawing a boundary is not 'what belongs together logically' but 'which design decisions are likely to change independently' — Parnas's insight, which is often at odds with the flowchart-shaped decomposition most people draw first.
benefits: Change impact is contained: a design decision lives inside one module and is edited there.
Modules can be developed by separate groups in parallel with little negotiation (Parnas).
The system can be understood one module at a time rather than all at once.
A drastic internal change (new data structure, new algorithm) requires no change outside the module.
Build times, test fixtures and ownership boundaries all follow from the cut.
tradeoffs: Perfect cohesion is unattainable and maximising it can create too many tiny modules with a disproportionate interface surface.
Data sharing can be genuinely cheaper than copying; low coupling is not free.
An information-hiding interface still requires an argument conversion or copy on every call, so the boundary has a runtime cost.
Cohesion and low coupling can pull in opposite directions — splitting a highly cohesive procedure to reduce its coupling is a regression.
The judgement about which decisions will change is a forecast, and forecasts are exactly what YAGNI warns about.
quality_attributes_note: coupling 9 means strong coupling *discipline* (low actual coupling, scored as a positive attribute); the axis name is ambiguous so read it as 'how well coupling is controlled'. testability 9 because module-level tests need only the module's own fixtures.

participants.responsibility: Holds one design decision behind an abstract interface; the unit of independent change.
participants.notes: Parnas: each module keeps its own secret — a design decision about some aspect of the system.

participants.responsibility: The stable contract that reveals the module's unchanging aspects and hides its varying ones.
participants.notes: Must permit one implementation to be replaced by another with no effect outside.

participants.responsibility: Depends only on the interface, never on the implementation behind it.
participants.notes: The asymmetry — strong coupling inside the module, weak coupling at the interface — is the point.

use_cases: Splitting a `Rectangle` that both computes area and renders, so geometry no longer depends on the GUI.
Cutting a monolith into packages that each own a schema fragment.
Putting a shared global into a module that owns it, so readers stop importing it directly.
Separating a volatile third-party SDK behind an adapter module.
Moving configuration out of every module that read a file into one configuration module.
avoid_when: The module would become a single-use pass-through to a module three hops away.
Splitting a small, genuinely cohesive procedure to satisfy a coupling metric.
The data is large and read-only, and copying it across the boundary costs more than the coupling saves.
You cannot identify any decision in the module that is likely to change — then there is no secret to hide.
pitfalls: Splitting along the flowchart of the runtime flow rather than along the decisions that change.
A "shared" or "common" module that every other module depends on — the coupling has merely been collected.
Sharing data structures across module boundaries so the interface exposes the implementation.
Interfaces with more members than any client needs, which is coupling by another name.
Passing huge parameter objects around instead of passing an interface reference — coupling with extra steps.

related_patterns_notes.encapsulate-collection: The canonical concrete application of high cohesion: wrap the collection so callers traverse it through the module's own interface rather than its representation.
related_patterns_notes.conceptual-contour: Decomposes along the system's recurring conceptual lines — the domain-level companion to the technical criteria here.

anti_patterns: A `Utils`/`Common` module that every module imports (the "God module").
Global mutable state shared between modules instead of an explicit contract.
Passing a raw table, row or DTO across a boundary so the receiving module depends on the sender's representation.
Splitting a cohesive procedure purely to reduce a coupling metric.
A module whose interface exposes its data structure so callers traverse it directly.
design_principles: Begin with a list of difficult design decisions, or decisions likely to change; design each module to hide one such decision (Parnas 1972).
Modules should possess well-specified abstract interfaces and have high cohesion and low coupling (Schmidt).
Modules are abstractions that should be independent, have well-specified interfaces, and have high cohesion and low coupling (Schmidt).
Low coupling is achieved by designing for protected variation (Larman).
Cohesion measures the relationship among the responsibilities inside a module; coupling measures the strength of association between modules (Stevens, Myers, Constantine 1974).
best_practices: Choose the boundary by asking "which decision here is likely to change independently?" — not "which step of the flow is this?".
Declare an explicit interface for every module, even when the caller is in the same repository.
Directionally: coupling is asymmetric, so aim for strong coupling inside a module and weak coupling across its interface.
Keep shared knowledge in one owner and reference it; never duplicate it across module boundaries.
Prefer parameter passing and returned values over shared globals — that is the ordering of the coupling spectrum.
Re-measure cohesion and coupling after every structural change; both can degrade silently.
